note: Judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. A tool marked not run was scored from its description only, and a source marked not fetched was not read.

groups.job: Help desk (where customers write and where drafts are sent from)

recommendation.beginner: Use the help desk the client already has. If they have none, Chatwoot is a good first choice because Deskfern's webhook check for it was written from the vendor's own help article.
recommendation.implementer: Chatwoot is the best tested path here (signature check and send call against a stand in). Intercom, Zendesk and Freshdesk adapters are written from memory of public docs and need a test against the client's own account first.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Chatwoot is open source and can be hosted for the cost of a small server. The paid desks have their own price pages, read them yourself before choosing.
recommendation.open_source_when: Open source is the right call when the client wants conversations on their own server, or a team is small and can run Docker. It is the wrong call when support staff already live in Intercom, Zendesk or Freshdesk.

tools.name: Intercom
tools.supported_in_deskfern: Adapter written from memory, tested against a stand in

fit.evidence: Strong AI help desk with its own answer product, so Deskfern overlaps with it. Our adapter reads conversations and posts replies and notes.

setup.evidence: Needs an access token from the developer hub. Not run here, judged from the steps.

reliability.evidence: Mature hosted service with wide use.

cost.evidence: Per seat and per resolution pricing in general. Not read today, no figures quoted.

data.evidence: Data sits with the vendor, in the vendor's regions.

integration.evidence: Adapter covers list and reply only, written from memory and not run.

setup.evidence: Self hosting needs Docker, a database and an email setup. A hosted plan exists too.

reliability.evidence: Active project, but you own the upgrades when self hosted.

groups.job: Search index for the knowledge base

recommendation.beginner: Keep the built in SQLite search for a demo and for a small help centre. You do not need to set up anything else.
recommendation.implementer: Use SQLite full text for a single client on one server, Postgres full text when the client runs on Postgres. Add real embeddings only after you measure that keyword search misses too many questions (the held out numbers in this repo show it does for wording that differs from the pages).
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Both full text options cost nothing extra. A hosted vector database adds a monthly bill and a second place your data lives.
recommendation.open_source_when: Open source search is the right call for a help centre of a few thousand pages. A hosted vector database is worth it when meaning based search over a large, changing set matters more than cost.

tools.name: Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone)
tools.supported_in_deskfern: Not built. Deskfern uses a hashed word vector stand in

fit.evidence: Meaning based search finds pages that share no words with the question, which is the weakness measured in this repo.

setup.evidence: Needs an account, an index and a way to make embeddings.

reliability.evidence: Managed service. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

data.evidence: Documents and vectors leave your server.

tools.name: SQLite full text (FTS5)
tools.run: run in the tests and the demo

fit.evidence: Word matching with ranking. Misses questions that use other words than the page, as the held out set shows.

setup.evidence: Ships inside Python, nothing to install.

reliability.evidence: Very stable, runs in one file.

cost.evidence: Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

data.evidence: Data stays in your database file.

integration.evidence: Used directly, with a rebuild step.

tools.name: Postgres full text
tools.supported_in_deskfern: Built, SQL path exercised in a throwaway Postgres 17

fit.evidence: Same word matching idea as SQLite, with stemming rules of its own.

setup.evidence: Already there when the client runs Postgres.

reliability.evidence: Stable and widely run. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

cost.evidence: Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

data.evidence: Stays in your database. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

integration.evidence: Deskfern stores stems and queries them with to_tsvector.

tools.name: pgvector (Postgres extension)
tools.supported_in_deskfern: Not built. Not installed in the local Postgres used here

fit.evidence: Would allow meaning based search inside Postgres if embeddings are produced elsewhere.

setup.evidence: Needs the extension on the host. Not present in the local Postgres 17 used for tests, and host support is UNVERIFIED.

reliability.evidence: Well known extension. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

data.evidence: Stays in your database. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

recommendation.beginner: If the client takes cards with Stripe, use it. Keep MODE=draft until a person has approved a test refund in Stripe's test mode.
recommendation.implementer: Stripe is the only refund adapter. It is tested only against a stand in. Use a restricted key that can write refunds only, and keep the approval step on.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Refunds themselves are a normal part of the card processor's pricing. Check the current price page yourself.
recommendation.open_source_when: There is no open source way to refund a card payment. For other processors write an adapter from the recipe prompt.

tools.name: Stripe refunds
tools.supported_in_deskfern: Adapter tested against a stand in

fit.evidence: Create refund call matches what Deskfern needs: a charge, an amount, a reason and metadata.

setup.evidence: Needs a secret or restricted key. Test mode makes a safe first run.

cost.evidence: Priced as part of the processor. Not read today.

data.evidence: Payment data stays with Stripe, Deskfern stores only a charge id.

integration.evidence: Adapter sends an idempotency key so a retry cannot pay twice. Not run live.

recommendation.beginner: Start with a folder of Markdown or PDF files. It needs no account and is the best tested source.
recommendation.implementer: Use the folder source for anything you can export. Drive and Notion adapters are read only and written from memory, test each against the client's own workspace first.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: A folder costs nothing. Drive and Notion are usually already paid for by the client.
recommendation.open_source_when: A plain folder (or a Git repo of Markdown) is the right call when the client wants control and a clean history. Use Drive or Notion when staff already write the help pages there.

reliability.evidence: Reliable. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

data.evidence: Documents stay with Google, Deskfern stores a copy of the text.

integration.evidence: Lists documents and exports text. Written from memory, not run.

data.evidence: Pages stay with Notion, Deskfern stores a copy.

integration.evidence: Searches pages and reads block text. Written from memory, not run.

tools.name: Local folder (Markdown, text, PDF)
tools.run: run in the tests and the demo

fit.evidence: Covers the common case: exported help pages and policy PDFs. PDFs with scanned images are not read.

setup.evidence: Point it at a folder. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

reliability.evidence: Plain files, easy to back up and review.

cost.evidence: Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.

integration.evidence: Built into Deskfern, skips links that point outside the folder and files over 10 MB.

recommendation.beginner: Use the offline rules writer to try the product. It copies sentences from your pages, which is dull but never invents anything.
recommendation.implementer: Measure before you switch: run the held out questions and the test cases with the model writer in a test account, and keep the groundedness check on whatever writes the words.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: The offline writer costs nothing. A model writer costs per use. Read the price page yourself.
recommendation.open_source_when: There is no open source model scored here. Self hosted models are possible but were not tried.

integration.evidence: The writer interface exists and the groundedness check judges its output. Never run live.

recommendation.open_source_when: Self hosting is the right call when data must stay in one place you control. It costs your time for updates and backups.
